quests.definition: A common greeting used when meeting someone or starting a conversation.
quests.example: Hello, I'm calling about the apartment you listed online.
quests.usageExample: On the phone, a rising 'Hello?' means 'who's calling?' — different from a flat friendly 'Hello' in person.
quests.nativeTip: In British English, 'Hiya' is common among friends. In North America, 'Hey' or 'How's it going?' is standard.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'Hello' to acknowledge an order or answer 'Yes'. It is solely an introductory greeting.

teachingCards.title: Universal English Greeting
teachingCards.explanation: 'Hello' is the universal starting point for any English conversation. It is equally appropriate in casual coffee shops and executive boardroom meetings.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Combine 'Hello' with the listener's name or a greeting phrase ('Hello Sarah, how are you today?') for natural warmth.

quests.definition: A word of farewell said when leaving someone or ending a conversation.
quests.example: Goodbye — call me when you land safely.
quests.usageExample: Full 'Goodbye' can sound formal or final; 'Bye', 'See you soon', or 'Take care' are the everyday casual go-to choices.
quests.nativeTip: At the end of a workday, colleagues often say 'Have a good evening!' or 'See you tomorrow!' instead of 'Goodbye'.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'Goodnight' when meeting someone in the evening. 'Goodnight' means goodbye/going to sleep.

teachingCards.title: Departures and Farewells
teachingCards.explanation: 'Goodbye' signals closure. While grammatically perfect everywhere, native speakers usually prefer warmer variants in casual contexts.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'Have a good one!' is an extremely popular all-purpose friendly departure phrase in North America and Australia.

quests.definition: Used to make a request sound polite rather than like a command.
quests.example: Could you send me the invoice before five, please?
quests.usageExample: 'Please sit down' at the start sounds like an instruction, while 'Sit down, please' at the end sounds softer.
quests.nativeTip: English speakers consider 'Please' practically mandatory whenever requesting items in cafes, restaurants, or shops.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'Please' when offering or giving something (e.g. handing food). Use 'Here you go' instead.

teachingCards.title: The Golden Courtesy Word
teachingCards.explanation: Omitting 'Please' in English can unintentionally make reasonable requests sound demanding or rude to native ears.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: In workplace requests, combine 'Could you please...' with a specific time window for optimal professionalism.

quests.definition: A phrase used to express appreciation or gratitude to someone.
quests.example: Thank you for reviewing the proposal so quickly.
quests.usageExample: 'Thanks' is friendly and casual; 'Thank you very much' or 'I really appreciate it' adds genuine weight.
quests.nativeTip: Always acknowledge small favors (holding an elevator, handing a receipt) with a quick 'Thanks!' or 'Thank you'.
quests.visualAnchor: 🎁 Receiving assistance → 💖 Heartfelt gratitude → 🙏 Thank you
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'Thanks you' — it's either 'Thanks' or 'Thank you'.

teachingCards.title: Expressing Gratitude Naturally
teachingCards.explanation: 'Thank you' is universally welcomed in every sphere of life. In English-speaking cultures, over-thanking is better than forgetting to thank.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Add the reason to make it memorable: 'Thank you for your patience' transforms standard politeness into personal connection.

quests.definition: Feeling regret or sorrow; used to apologize or excuse oneself.
quests.example: I'm sorry for being late — the train was delayed.
quests.usageExample: 'Sorry' is used for major apologies, but also for small courtesies like bumping into someone or asking someone to repeat.
quests.nativeTip: In the UK and Canada, people say 'Sorry!' almost automatically when passing close to strangers.
quests.visualAnchor: ⚠️ Minor bump or delay → 🙇 Empathy & regret → 🤝 'Sorry!'
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'I'm sorry' if you didn't hear what someone said. 'Pardon?' or 'Sorry, could you repeat that?' is correct.

teachingCards.title: Navigating Apologies & Empathy
teachingCards.explanation: 'Sorry' handles three distinct roles in English: apologizing for errors, expressing empathy ('I'm so sorry to hear that'), and polite interruption.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: For professional emails, 'Thank you for your patience' is often more effective than repeated 'I am sorry for the delay'.

quests.definition: Used to give an affirmative response, agreement, or confirmation.
quests.example: Yes, I will be attending the workshop tomorrow.
quests.usageExample: In casual talk, native speakers frequently say 'Yeah', 'Yep', 'Sure', or 'Definitely'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Yes' followed by a slight pause sounds firm and decisive. In formal interviews, 'Yes, absolutely' shows great enthusiasm.
quests.commonMistake: Avoid answering 'Yes' when you mean 'I understand'. Use 'Got it' or 'I see' instead.

teachingCards.title: Clear Affirmation
teachingCards.explanation: 'Yes' gives clear, unambiguous confirmation. Tone of voice gives it either cheerful agreement or professional resolve.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Pairing 'Yes' with a short clause ('Yes, I did', 'Yes, that sounds great') sounds much more natural than a bare monosyllabic 'Yes'.

quests.definition: Used to give a negative response, refusal, or disagreement.
quests.example: No, we haven't received the shipment yet.
quests.usageExample: Direct 'No' can sound blunt in social requests; natives often soften it: 'I'm afraid not' or 'Not right now'.
quests.nativeTip: When declining offers (e.g. more coffee), 'No, thank you' or 'I'm good, thanks!' is the standard polite protocol.
quests.visualAnchor: ❌ Boundary or decline → ✋ Diplomatic refusal → 🙅 No
quests.commonMistake: Don't answer 'No' to negative questions unless you mean negative (e.g. 'You don't mind?' -> 'No, not at all' means you agree).

teachingCards.title: Diplomatic Refusal
teachingCards.explanation: Saying 'No' without causing offense is an art in English. Cushioning with gratitude ('No, but thank you!') keeps communication warm.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: In professional negotiations, 'That won't be possible at this stage' is preferred over a blunt 'No'.

quests.definition: To assist or provide what is necessary to accomplish a task.
quests.example: Could you help me move this table to the conference room?
quests.usageExample: 'Help!' shouted alone is an emergency cry. 'Can I help you?' is a friendly service offer.
quests.nativeTip: In retail or customer service, 'How can I help you today?' is the quintessential greeting.
quests.visualAnchor: 🆘 Heavy task / emergency → 🤝 Extended hand → 💡 Help
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'Give me a help'. The natural idiom is 'Give me a hand' or 'Help me out'.

teachingCards.title: Requesting and Offering Support
teachingCards.explanation: 'Help' functions both as an urgent alert and a collaborative workplace tool. Tone determines urgency.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Asking 'Could you lend me a hand with this?' sounds friendly and team-oriented in office environments.

quests.definition: A clear, colorless liquid essential for all plant and animal life.
quests.example: Would you like a glass of water while you wait?
quests.usageExample: In restaurants, specify 'Still water' (flat) vs 'Sparkling water' (bubbly) or 'Tap water' (free tap).
quests.nativeTip: American English pronounces the 't' as a soft flap /d/ ('wah-der'); British English pronounces a sharp crisp /t/.
quests.commonMistake: 'Water' is uncountable. Never say 'two waters' unless referring to glasses/bottles in an informal cafe order.

teachingCards.title: Everyday Dining Essential
teachingCards.explanation: Mastering how to request water smoothly in restaurants avoids awkward beverage billing abroad.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Asking for 'tap water' in North America and the UK is completely normal and free of charge.

quests.definition: Any nutritious substance that people or animals eat to maintain life and growth.
quests.example: The local market has incredible street food from around the world.
quests.usageExample: 'Food' is general; 'Meal' refers to a specific sitting (breakfast, lunch, dinner); 'Dish' refers to a recipe.
quests.nativeTip: Native speakers love talking about food culture: 'Are you a foodie?' means 'Do you love discovering new cuisines?'.
quests.commonMistake: 'Food' is uncountable in everyday use. Don't say 'I bought three foods'. Say 'I bought some groceries/food'.

teachingCards.title: Food, Dishes & Meals
teachingCards.explanation: Distinguish between 'food' (the substance), 'dish' (a specific prepared recipe), and 'meal' (the dining occasion).
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: When complimenting a host, say 'The food is delicious!' or 'This dish is amazing!'.

quests.definition: The place where one lives permanently, especially as a member of a family or household.
quests.example: After a long travel week, it feels so good to be home.
quests.usageExample: 'House' is the physical brick structure; 'Home' is the emotional place of comfort and belonging.
quests.nativeTip: We say 'go home' or 'stay home' WITHOUT 'to' (never say 'go to home').
quests.commonMistake: Never say 'I am going to home'. The preposition 'to' is omitted with home: 'I am going home'.

teachingCards.title: House vs Home
teachingCards.explanation: 'House' is real estate; 'Home' is feelings, memories, and sanctuary. English grammar treats 'home' as an adverb of direction.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'Make yourself at home!' is the warmest greeting you can give a guest stepping into your apartment.

quests.definition: An institution for educating children or offering specialized training.
quests.example: The children walk to school together every morning.
quests.usageExample: In American English, 'school' can also refer to university ('Where did you go to school?').
quests.nativeTip: Like 'home', we say 'go to school' without an article (never 'go to the school' unless visiting the building).
quests.commonMistake: Say 'at school' when attending classes, not 'in the school'.

teachingCards.title: Educational Institutions
teachingCards.explanation: Using or omitting 'the' changes meaning: 'He is in prison / at school' means he is a prisoner / student. 'He is at the school' means he is physically visiting.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Americans casually ask adults 'What did you study in school?' meaning college or university.

quests.definition: A person whom one knows and with whom one has a bond of mutual affection.
quests.example: She has been my closest friend since our college days.
quests.usageExample: English distinguishes 'acquaintance' (casual contact), 'friend' (good companion), and 'close friend' (trusted confidant).
quests.nativeTip: 'Make friends' is the collocation (never 'do friends' or 'build friends').
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'friend of me'. Use the double possessive: 'a friend of mine'.

teachingCards.title: Social Bonds & Collocations
teachingCards.explanation: Native speakers are deliberate about who they call a 'close friend' versus an 'acquaintance' or 'colleague'.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Use 'a friend of mine' when introducing someone casually in conversation.

quests.definition: To be desired or approved of; having the required qualities or high standard.
quests.example: That's a really good suggestion for the presentation.
quests.usageExample: When asked 'How are you?', native speakers frequently answer 'Good!' in everyday casual settings.
quests.nativeTip: To elevate from basic English, upgrade 'good' to 'exceptional', 'solid', 'effective', or 'valuable' in business.
quests.commonMistake: 'Good' is an adjective ('He is a good player'); 'Well' is an adverb ('He plays well').

teachingCards.title: Good vs Well
teachingCards.explanation: Use 'good' to describe people, places, and things (nouns). Use 'well' to describe actions (verbs).
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: In professional writing, replacing 'good results' with 'impressive results' or 'robust metrics' immediately elevates your tone.

quests.definition: Of poor quality or a low standard; not desirable or favorable.
quests.example: Heavy rain caused bad traffic conditions across the city.
quests.usageExample: 'My bad' is a very popular casual idiom meaning 'that was my fault / my mistake'.
quests.nativeTip: In professional feedback, avoid blunt 'That's bad' — use 'There is room for improvement' or 'This needs revision'.
quests.visualAnchor: 🌧️ Storm cloud → 📉 Drop in quality → ⚠️ Bad
quests.commonMistake: 'Feel bad' means experiencing guilt/sympathy ('I feel bad for him'). 'Feel badly' is grammatically non-standard.

teachingCards.title: Expressing Criticism Diplomatically
teachingCards.explanation: English workplace culture softens negative evaluations. Saying 'It is not quite there yet' is preferred over 'This is bad'.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'My bad!' is perfect for minor social oopsies (stepping on someone's foot, spilling a drop of water).

quests.definition: Feeling or showing pleasure, contentment, or satisfaction.
quests.example: We are very happy with the team's progress this quarter.
quests.usageExample: 'Happy' is standard contentment; 'Thrilled' is energetic excitement; 'Content' is calm peace.
quests.nativeTip: In professional emails, 'I'd be happy to assist with that' is a warm and courteous commitment.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'Happy for you to meet'. Say 'Happy to meet you'.

teachingCards.title: Emotional Nuance: Joy & Satisfaction
teachingCards.explanation: 'Happy' spans everything from casual satisfaction to profound joy. Pairing it with prepositions ('happy with', 'happy about') clarifies context.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'More than happy to help!' is one of the highest-rated customer service phrases in English.

quests.definition: Feeling or showing sorrow; unhappy or mournful.
quests.example: It was sad to see our favorite neighborhood bookstore close down.
quests.usageExample: 'Sad' is common; 'Down in the dumps' is an idiom for temporary low mood; 'Devastated' is intense grief.
quests.nativeTip: When sympathizing with someone's bad news, say 'I'm so sad to hear that' or 'That must be really tough'.
quests.commonMistake: Saying 'a sad person' can sound pitying; native speakers prefer 'He is going through a tough time'.

teachingCards.title: Expressing Sympathy and Low Spirits
teachingCards.explanation: English offers gentle ways to acknowledge sadness without being intrusive. Listening empathetically matters most.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Use 'I'm thinking of you' or 'Sending you warm thoughts' when someone shares sad news.

quests.definition: Of considerable size, extent, or intensity.
quests.example: Deciding to relocate across the country is a big decision.
quests.usageExample: 'Big' carries emotional weight ('big deal', 'big mistake'); 'Large' is neutral and factual ('large shipment').
quests.nativeTip: Never say 'a large deal' — native speakers always say 'a big deal' because 'big' emphasizes emotional importance.
quests.commonMistake: Don't use 'big' for body height; say 'tall', not 'a big man' (which implies broad/heavy).

teachingCards.title: Big vs Large: Emotion vs Fact
teachingCards.explanation: 'Big' adds drama and personal stakes (a big surprise, a big opportunity). 'Large' sounds objective and measured.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'No big deal' is the quintessential English way to say 'Don't worry about it at all!'.

quests.definition: Of a size that is less than normal or usual; not great in amount or degree.
quests.example: Let's start with a small pilot project before expanding.
quests.usageExample: 'Small' refers to physical dimensions or significance; 'Tiny' means extremely small; 'Petite' refers to slender people.
quests.nativeTip: In conversations, 'small talk' refers to casual friendly chats about light topics like weather or weekend plans.
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse 'small' and 'short'. For human height, always use 'short'.

teachingCards.title: Small vs Little
teachingCards.explanation: 'Small' is strictly factual and measurable. 'Little' often conveys affection or emotional tenderness ('my little sister').
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Mastering 'small talk' is considered a vital networking and workplace skill in international business.

quests.definition: Having a high degree of heat or a high temperature.
quests.example: Be careful with that tea kettle — it's extremely hot.
quests.usageExample: 'Hot' can mean temperature, spicy flavor ('hot sauce'), or trending popularity ('hot new startup').
quests.nativeTip: In food, clarify: 'Do you mean hot temperature or spicy hot?' to avoid accidental chili surprises.
quests.commonMistake: 'I am hot' means you feel physically warm. Be careful with tone as it can informally mean attractive in slang.

teachingCards.title: Temperature, Flavor & Idioms
teachingCards.explanation: 'Hot' works across physical heat, spicy culinary heat, and cultural popularity.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'A hot topic' means a current subject that everyone is enthusiastically debating right now.

quests.definition: Of or at a low or relatively low temperature.
quests.example: Dress warmly today; the wind makes it feel freezing cold outside.
quests.usageExample: 'Cold' describes weather, but also aloof demeanor: 'She gave me a cold reception'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Catch a cold' is the medical idiom (meaning minor viral illness). 'Have cold feet' means becoming nervous before a big event.
quests.commonMistake: Say 'I am cold' (you feel chilled). Don't say 'I have cold' — that means you caught a virus ('I have a cold').

teachingCards.title: Chilly Weather vs Emotional Distance
teachingCards.explanation: Describing someone as 'cold' means they are unapproachable or unempathetic. Context makes the difference clear.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'Cold calling' in sales means reaching out to prospective clients without any prior introduction.

quests.definition: A period of twenty-four hours or the time between sunrise and sunset.
quests.example: Have a wonderful day at your new job!
quests.usageExample: 'Call it a day' is one of the most common workplace idioms, meaning 'let's stop working for today'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Day in and day out' means continuously repeating an action without taking breaks.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'yesterday day'. Simply say 'yesterday' or 'yesterday morning'.

teachingCards.title: Temporal Routines & Daily Life
teachingCards.explanation: 'Day' underpins dozens of natural English idioms for scheduling, pacing, and productivity.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Ending a meeting with 'Let's call it a day, team!' signals high satisfaction and wrap-up.

quests.definition: The period of darkness in each twenty-four hours; the time between sunset and sunrise.
quests.example: The city looks completely mesmerizing from above at night.
quests.usageExample: Remember: 'Good evening' is a greeting when you arrive; 'Goodnight' is exclusively a farewell when leaving or sleeping.
quests.nativeTip: 'An all-nighter' is an informal term for staying awake all night to study or complete a project.
quests.commonMistake: Never greet someone at 8 PM by saying 'Goodnight!'. Say 'Good evening!' instead.

teachingCards.title: Evening vs Night Etiquette
teachingCards.explanation: The crucial distinction: 'Good evening' opens conversations at night; 'Good night' closes conversations.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'Pulling an all-nighter' is a badge of honor among university students and hackathon participants.

quests.definition: To move from one place to another; to travel or proceed.
quests.example: Let's go to the main conference hall before the keynote starts.
quests.usageExample: Irregular past tense: 'go' -> 'went' -> 'gone'. Pairing with prepositions changes meaning ('go on', 'go out', 'go over').
quests.nativeTip: 'Let me give it a go' means 'Let me try it out or attempt it'.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'go to shopping'. Use 'go shopping' or 'go swimming' without 'to'.

teachingCards.title: Movement & Core Verbs
teachingCards.explanation: 'Go' is one of the most versatile action verbs in English. It forms vital phrasal verbs like 'go ahead' (proceed).
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Saying 'Here we go!' adds playful momentum before starting a challenging task.

quests.definition: To put food into the mouth and chew and swallow it.
quests.example: We usually eat lunch together in the office courtyard.
quests.usageExample: Irregular forms: 'eat' -> 'ate' (/eɪt/) -> 'eaten'. Phrasal verb 'eat out' means dining at a restaurant.
quests.nativeTip: 'Grab a bite to eat' is the universally preferred casual invitation over formal 'Shall we consume food?'.
quests.commonMistake: Don't say 'eat medicine'. In English, you 'take medicine'.

teachingCards.title: Culinary Collocations & Social Invitations
teachingCards.explanation: Socializing in English often centers on eating. Knowing casual invitation idioms makes connecting easy.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'Let's grab a bite!' is friendly, low-pressure, and perfect for catching up with peers.

quests.definition: To take liquid into the mouth and swallow it.
quests.example: Make sure you drink plenty of fluids while running in this heat.
quests.usageExample: Irregular forms: 'drink' -> 'drank' -> 'drunk'. Used as a noun: 'Would you like a warm drink?'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Grab a drink' after work is common professional socializing (can be coffee, tea, or juice, not just alcohol).
quests.commonMistake: Don't confuse 'drank' (past simple) and 'drunk' (past participle): 'I drank water', 'I have drunk water'.

teachingCards.title: Beverage Culture & Socializing
teachingCards.explanation: 'Going for a drink' is a cornerstone of professional relationship building across the English-speaking world.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: If you don't drink alcohol, simply ordering a sparkling water with lime fits in effortlessly.

quests.definition: A condition of body and mind that recurs for several hours every night.
quests.example: I need to get at least seven hours of sleep before the presentation.
quests.usageExample: Irregular forms: 'sleep' -> 'slept' -> 'slept'. Idiom: 'Let me sleep on it' means 'Let me decide tomorrow'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Sleep like a log' means sleeping very deeply and peacefully without waking up.
quests.commonMistake: 'Sleep' is the state ('I am sleeping'). 'Fall asleep' is the transition from awake to asleep.

teachingCards.title: Sleep Idioms in Business & Life
teachingCards.explanation: 'Let me sleep on it' is a polite, professional way to delay signing an agreement without saying no outright.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: Native speakers frequently praise restorative sleep: 'I feel completely recharged after that good night's sleep!'.

quests.definition: To mark letters, words, or symbols on a surface, typically paper or screen.
quests.example: Please write down your contact details on the sign-in sheet.
quests.usageExample: Irregular forms: 'write' -> 'wrote' -> 'written'. Silent 'w' at the start: pronounced /raɪt/, exactly like 'right'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Drop me a line' is a friendly classic idiom meaning 'write me a quick email or message'.
quests.visualAnchor: ✍️ Pen on paper → 📝 Clear notes → 💻 Write
quests.commonMistake: Homophones: 'write' (create text), 'right' (correct / direction), 'rite' (ceremony). Don't confuse spelling.

teachingCards.title: Written Communication
teachingCards.explanation: Clear writing is the hallmark of modern professional English. Silent consonants like the 'w' in 'write' are common.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'Write back when you have a free moment!' is a courteous way to conclude casual correspondence.

quests.definition: To look at and comprehend the meaning of written or printed characters.
quests.example: I always read the morning news brief with my cup of coffee.
quests.usageExample: Fascinating verb: spelled identically in present and past ('read'), but present sounds like 'reed' and past sounds like 'red'.
quests.nativeTip: 'Read between the lines' means discovering the hidden subtext or true meaning not explicitly stated.
quests.commonMistake: Remember the vowel sound shift: 'Today I /riːd/', but 'Yesterday I /rɛd/'.

teachingCards.title: The Dual-Pronunciation Verb
teachingCards.explanation: 'Read' is spelled the same in all three tenses (read, read, read), but the vowel sound changes between present and past.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'I read you loud and clear!' is a popular radio-derived phrase meaning 'I understand your message completely'.

quests.definition: To say words in order to express one's thoughts and feelings; to communicate orally.
quests.example: She can speak three languages with complete fluency.
quests.usageExample: Irregular forms: 'speak' -> 'spoke' -> 'spoken'. 'Speak with' is collaborative; 'speak to' can sound more directional.
quests.nativeTip: 'Actions speak louder than words' is one of the most widely quoted proverbs in the English language.
quests.commonMistake: 'Speak' refers to language ability ('I speak English'). Don't say 'I talk English'.

teachingCards.title: Speak vs Talk
teachingCards.explanation: Use 'speak' for languages and formal speeches ('He spoke at the conference'). Use 'talk' for casual social chatter.
teachingCards.nativeSpeakerInsight: 'So to speak' is used when describing something metaphorically or figuratively.
